q: What file format are ARM templates written in?
exp: ARM templates are written in JSON, with a $schema, parameters, variables, resources and outputs. Bicep is a separate language that compiles to that JSON. YAML, XML and HCL (used by Terraform) aren't ARM template formats.

q: Which template function returns the location of the resource group being deployed to?
exp: resourceGroup().location returns the region of the resource group you're deploying to. It's commonly used as the default value of a location parameter, so resources land in the same region as their resource group. subscription() has no location, and deployment() and location() don't return it.

q: Which template function builds a globally unique storage account name from the resource group ID?
exp: uniqueString(resourceGroup().id) returns a 13-character hash based on the resource group ID. It's the same every time for the same resource group but different across resource groups, which makes names unique and repeatable. Combine it with a prefix, such as concat('st', uniqueString(...)). guid() and random() aren't suitable, and newName() doesn't exist.

q: A VM resource must deploy only after its NIC exists. Which property ensures this in ARM JSON?
exp: dependsOn lists resources that must be deployed first. Adding the NIC's resource ID to the VM's dependsOn makes Resource Manager create the NIC before the VM. condition decides whether to deploy at all, copy creates multiple instances, and apiVersion picks the API version.

q: You need to deploy 5 identical storage accounts from one resource definition. Which ARM element?
exp: The copy element repeats a resource definition: copy: { name: 'storageLoop', count: 5 } deploys five instances, and copyIndex() gives each one a different name. dependsOn sets order, outputs return values, and condition deploys or skips a resource.

q: A parameter must accept only 'Standard_LRS' or 'Standard_GRS'. Which parameter property enforces this?
exp: allowedValues lists the only values a parameter accepts. Deployment fails with any other value. defaultValue sets the value when none is given, metadata adds a description, and minLength checks string length.

q: How should you supply an admin password to a template deployment without storing the password itself in plain text in the parameter file?
opts: Reference a Key Vault secret from the parameter file
exp: A parameter file can reference a Key Vault secret (by the vault's resource ID and the secret name) instead of containing the password. At deployment, Resource Manager reads the secret from the vault, so the password never appears in plain text. Hard-coding it, outputting it or putting it in tags exposes it.

q: A deployment referencing a Key Vault secret fails with an access error. Which vault setting is likely missing?
opts: Azure Resource Manager for template deployment (enabledForTemplateDeployment)
exp: For a template to read a secret during deployment, the key vault must have 'Azure Resource Manager for template deployment' enabled (enabledForTemplateDeployment), and the person deploying needs permission on the vault. Soft delete, purge protection and private endpoints don't control this.

q: What's the purpose of a parameter file (azuredeploy.parameters.json)?
opts: Supply environment-specific values to a template without editing it
exp: A parameter file holds the values for a template's parameters, so the same template can be deployed to dev, test and prod by passing different parameter files, without editing the template. It doesn't define resources or store logs, and it can't replace the template.

q: Which CLI command deploys a template at subscription scope (for example, to create resource groups)?
opts: az deployment sub create --location westeurope --template-file main.json
exp: az deployment sub create deploys a template at subscription scope — for example to create resource groups or assign policies. It needs --location because the deployment's metadata is stored in a region. az deployment group create targets an existing resource group, and az deployment tenant create targets the tenant root.

q: You redeploy the same template with identical parameters in Incremental mode. What happens to existing resources?
opts: They're left as is or updated to match the template (idempotent)
The deployment fails because the resources exist
exp: ARM deployments are idempotent. Redeploying the same template with the same parameters leaves matching resources as they are, updates any settings that differ, and creates nothing extra. Resources aren't deleted and recreated, the deployment doesn't fail, and no duplicates appear.

q: Where in the portal can you see past deployments and their templates for a resource group?
exp: Resource group → Deployments lists every deployment to that resource group, with its status, inputs, outputs and the template used, which you can download or redeploy. The Activity log shows individual operations but not the full template.

q: A resource should deploy only when the parameter deployDiagnostics is true. Which ARM property?
exp: The condition property deploys a resource only when its value is true, for example "condition": "[parameters('deployDiagnostics')]". When it's false, the resource is skipped and the rest of the deployment continues. dependsOn, copy and outputs don't do this.

q: In a template, an output returns the public IP address after deployment. Which section?
exp: The outputs section returns values after deployment, for example the public IP address via reference(...).ipAddress. Variables are internal values, parameters are inputs, and functions define user-defined functions.

q: Which ARM template property must every resource definition include?
exp: Every resource in an ARM template needs type (such as Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts), apiVersion and name. Most resource types also need location. dependsOn, tags and copy are optional.

q: You want to reuse a shared networking template inside a main template. Which technique?
opts: Copy the JSON into every template
exp: A Microsoft.Resources/deployments resource deploys another template inside the main one: nested (inline) or linked (referenced by URI or template spec). This lets you keep the networking template separate and reuse it. Copying JSON creates duplicate code, and tags or Azure Policy can't include templates.

q: Where must a linked template file be stored for ARM to reach it during deployment?
opts: A URI accessible to Resource Manager (for example, a storage account with a SAS token) or use a template spec
exp: A linked template must be reachable by Resource Manager during deployment, so it needs a URI such as a storage account URL with a SAS token. Alternatively store it as a template spec, or use relativePath with a template spec or Bicep module. Files on your own disk can't be reached by ARM.

q: Which feature stores a versioned ARM template as an Azure resource so teams can deploy it with RBAC control?
exp: A template spec stores an ARM template (or Bicep, compiled) as an Azure resource, with version numbers. You control who can deploy it with Azure RBAC, which makes it easy to share approved templates across teams. Export template only generates a template, and policy initiatives group policies.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: A template can contain parameters with default values
Outputs can return secureString values safely in the history
The $schema property identifies the template language version
exp: Parameters can have default values, and variables can reference parameters. Don't output secrets, because outputs are stored in deployment history in plain text. The $schema property tells Azure which version of the template language the file uses.

q: Order the steps to safely deploy an updated template to production:
items: Run a what-if operation and review changes
Edit the template and parameter file
Validate the template (az deployment group validate)
exp: Edit the template and parameter file first. Validate them (az deployment group validate) to catch errors. Run what-if to see exactly what will change. Only then deploy with az deployment group create. Validation and what-if before deploying catch mistakes before they reach production.

q: Which keyword declares an input parameter in Bicep?
exp: param declares an input parameter in Bicep, for example param location string = resourceGroup().location. var declares a variable, resource declares a resource, and output returns a value. input and arg aren't Bicep keywords.

q: Which decorator restricts a Bicep parameter to a list of values?
exp: The @allowed decorator lists the values a parameter may take, for example @allowed(['Standard_LRS', 'Standard_GRS']); any other value fails validation. @values, @enum and @restrict aren't Bicep decorators.

q: How do you mark a Bicep parameter so its value isn't logged?
exp: @secure() on a string or object parameter makes it a secure value: it isn't logged in deployment history or returned in outputs. Use it for passwords and keys. The other decorators don't exist.

q: Which command deploys a Bicep file to a resource group?
opts: az deployment group create -g RG1 --template-file main.bicep
exp: az deployment group create --template-file main.bicep deploys a Bicep file directly; the CLI compiles it to ARM JSON automatically before sending it to Resource Manager. az bicep and bicep commands build and decompile but don't deploy.

q: In Bicep, how are dependencies between resources usually handled?
opts: Automatically, when one resource references another's symbolic name or properties
exp: In Bicep, when one resource uses another's symbolic name or properties (for example nic.id), Bicep adds the dependency automatically. You only write dependsOn for dependencies that can't be inferred. copy is ARM JSON syntax.

q: Which Bicep syntax creates 3 storage accounts in a loop?
exp: Bicep loops use [for item in collection: {...}]. range(0, 3) gives 0, 1 and 2, so this deploys three storage accounts, and you use i to make each name unique. copy: { count: 3 } is ARM JSON syntax, and the other forms aren't valid Bicep.

q: How do you deploy a resource conditionally in Bicep?
exp: In Bicep you add if (condition) after the = in a resource declaration, for example resource diag '...' = if (deployIt) { ... }. The resource is deployed only when the condition is true. condition: is ARM JSON, and @if and when don't exist.

q: Which keyword references another Bicep file as a reusable component?
exp: module deploys another Bicep file as part of your deployment: you pass it parameters and can read its outputs. It's how you split Bicep into reusable building blocks. import, include and template aren't the keyword for this.

q: How do you reference an EXISTING storage account (not deploy it) in Bicep to read its properties?
exp: Adding the existing keyword (resource stg '...' existing = { name: 'st1' }) references a resource that's already deployed, so you can read its properties such as stg.properties.primaryEndpoints without deploying or changing it. reference() is ARM JSON, and import and module don't do this.

q: You exported a resource group as an ARM JSON template. How do you get a Bicep version of it?
opts: Run az bicep decompile on the exported JSON
exp: az bicep decompile turns an ARM JSON template, such as one from Export template, into a .bicep file. Review it afterwards, because exported templates often contain hard-coded values. Renaming the file doesn't change its syntax, and az bicep build converts Bicep to JSON, not the other way.

q: What's the newer Bicep-native alternative to JSON parameter files?
exp: A .bicepparam file is a Bicep-native parameter file. It starts with using 'main.bicep' and sets values with param name = value, so the tooling checks types against the template. JSON parameter files still work. YAML, .tfvars (Terraform) and .env aren't Bicep parameter files.

q: Answer Yes or No about Bicep:
stmts: Bicep needs state files like Terraform
Bicep supports the same resource types and API versions as ARM
You can use what-if with Bicep deployments
Bicep output is visible in deployment history like ARM
exp: Bicep doesn't need a state file like Terraform — Azure itself holds the current state. It supports every resource type and API version that ARM does, from day one. What-if works with Bicep, and its outputs appear in deployment history just like ARM.

q: What determines a VM's vCPU count and memory?
exp: The VM size (for example Standard_D4s_v5) sets the number of vCPUs, the amount of memory, temp storage, how many data disks and NICs you can attach, and the network bandwidth. The disk type sets storage performance, the image sets the operating system, and the region doesn't change CPU or memory.

q: Which VM size family is optimized for memory-intensive workloads like large databases?
exp: E-series and M-series VMs have a high ratio of memory to CPU, which suits databases and in-memory analytics (M-series offers the most memory). F-series is compute-optimised, B-series is burstable for light workloads, and N-series has GPUs.

q: A low-traffic dev web server has occasional CPU spikes. Which size family is cheapest and suitable?
exp: B-series (burstable) VMs run at a low baseline cost and build up CPU credits while idle, which they spend on short spikes. That's cheap for low-traffic dev servers. M-series is large and memory-heavy, N-series has GPUs, and H-series is for high-performance computing — all far too expensive here.

q: A VM needs a GPU for machine learning training. Which family?
exp: N-series VMs include NVIDIA or AMD GPUs for machine learning training, rendering and visualisation. D-series is general-purpose, A-series is entry-level, and B-series is burstable; none of them have GPUs.

q: VMs must run a startup script that installs IIS automatically at first boot. Which features can do this?
opts: Custom Script Extension or cloud-init/custom data
exp: The Custom Script Extension runs a script after the VM is deployed, on Windows or Linux — for example to install IIS. On Linux, cloud-init via custom data can configure the VM at first boot. Boot diagnostics, Advisor and the serial console don't automate setup.

q: Which PowerShell cmdlet creates a VM?
exp: New-AzVM creates a virtual machine in Azure PowerShell, either with a simple parameter set (name, image, credentials) or from a full VM configuration object. The other cmdlet names don't exist.

q: You need to create many VMs from a customized Windows image and share the image across subscriptions with versioning. Which service?
exp: Azure Compute Gallery stores image definitions with numbered versions, replicates them to the regions you choose, and can be shared with other subscriptions or tenants through RBAC. That's ideal for building many VMs from one customised image. Loose VHDs in a storage account have no versioning or sharing, and a template doesn't capture an OS image.

q: Before capturing a reusable generalized Windows image, what must you run inside the VM?
exp: Before capturing a generalized Windows image, run Sysprep with the generalize option to remove machine-specific details such as the computer SID. Then each VM created from the image gets its own identity. On Linux, use waagent -deprovision. chkdsk, ipconfig and gpupdate don't prepare images.

q: Which disk type is cheapest and suits dev/test or infrequent access?
exp: Standard HDD is the cheapest managed disk type and suits dev/test, backups and rarely used data, where low performance doesn't matter. Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk cost more and are meant for production workloads that need fast, consistent IOPS.

q: What happens to data on the temporary disk (D: on Windows) when a VM is deallocated?
opts: It's moved to the OS disk
exp: The temporary disk (D: on Windows, /dev/sdb on many Linux images) is local storage on the physical host. When the VM is deallocated, redeployed or moved to another host, that data can be lost. Use it only for scratch data such as the page file, and keep anything important on managed data disks.

q: Which CLI command attaches a new 128 GB data disk to VM1?
opts: az vm disk attach -g RG1 --vm-name VM1 --name data1 --new --size-gb 128
exp: az vm disk attach attaches a data disk to a VM; with --new and --size-gb 128 it creates a new 128 GB managed disk and attaches it in one step. The other commands don't exist. After attaching, initialise and format the disk inside the OS.

q: Can you shrink a managed disk from 256 GB to 128 GB?
opts: No — managed disks can only be increased in size
exp: Managed disks can only grow, never shrink. To use a smaller disk, create a new one, copy the data across inside the VM, and swap it in. That applies to every disk type, whether or not the VM is running.

q: After expanding a data disk in Azure, what else must you do?
opts: Extend the partition/volume inside the guest OS
exp: Expanding a disk in Azure only makes the virtual disk bigger. The operating system still sees the old partition size until you extend the partition and file system — for example with Disk Management or diskpart on Windows, or growpart and resize2fs on Linux. You don't need to reinstall or recreate anything.

q: Two VMs in a failover cluster must attach the same managed disk at the same time. Which feature?
exp: Shared disks are managed disks with maxShares set above 1, so several VMs can attach the same disk at the same time. Clustered applications such as Windows Server Failover Clustering use them, managing who writes with SCSI reservations. Snapshots are copies, and Azure Files is a network share rather than a block disk.

q: You need a point-in-time copy of a VM's OS disk before patching. What's the fastest option?
exp: A disk snapshot is a full, read-only point-in-time copy of a managed disk that takes seconds to start. If patching goes wrong, create a new disk from the snapshot and swap it in. Capturing an image with Sysprep generalises (and changes) the VM, and exporting a template doesn't copy disk contents.

q: Which disk caching setting is recommended for SQL Server log disks?
exp: SQL Server log files are written sequentially and must be safely on disk immediately, so log disks should use caching None. Data disks usually use ReadOnly caching to speed up reads, and the OS disk uses ReadWrite. ReadWrite on a log disk risks losing data if the host fails.

q: Which feature lets a VM's OS disk be stored on the local host's cache or temp disk for fast, stateless reimaging?
exp: Ephemeral OS disks are stored on the host's local cache or temp disk, so they're free and very fast, and reimaging is quick. The trade-off is that data is lost on reimage, and the VM can't be stopped and deallocated. Ultra disks and shared disks are remote managed disks, and snapshots are backups.

q: Answer Yes or No about managed disks:
stmts: Managed disks are always encrypted at rest with SSE
You can change a disk from Standard SSD to Premium SSD
Disk type changes can be done while the VM is running in all cases
A snapshot can be used to create a new managed disk
exp: Managed disks are always encrypted at rest with server-side encryption. You can change a disk from Standard SSD to Premium SSD, but in most cases the VM must be deallocated first. A snapshot can be used to create a new managed disk.
